full_judgment:
6. Then, Mr Siddique places another aspect of the provisions of section 6(5) of the Ain, 2003 before this Court and submits that following passing a decree by the Artha Rin Adalat, the status of all the defendants become same in that the decree will be passed against all the defendants 'jointly' and 'severally' and, thus, if this petitioner remains as a defendant in the suit, she will encounter unbearable sufferings for no fault of her own. To elaborate the above facet of his submission, he explains that once the decree is passed by the Artha Rin Adalat against the petitioner, her name will be published in the Bangladesh Bank CIB List as a defaulter, on top of the fact that the Bank shall be pursuing further steps for repayment of loan, including putting her in civil imprisonment. Thus, keeping the petitioner on record as a principal defendant in her personal capacity, Mr Siddique submits, exposes her to a great risk of depriving her from most of the civil rights and practically depriving her from earning a living by lawful occupation, trade or business which are her fundamental rights enshrined in the Constitution. 

 10. He then submits that if the mortgaged property is taken to be the personal property of the mortgagor and whatever the claim or right of the creditor Bank may have against such mortgaged property, it is a right in rem and not a right in personal. As such, according to him, any claim of the creditor Bank is limited to the extent of the mortgaged property only. He forcefully argues that where the right of the lender-Bank over the mortgaged property is only a right in rem, no personal decree against the heir of the mortgagor can be passed under the provision of the Ain, 2003 in the light of the fact that the petitioner has no personal liability against the loan under Artha Rin suit No. 1 of 2011. 

 11. Mr Siddique also places the provisions of section 5(2) & 5(3) in tandem with Order 34 rules 2-6 of the CPC and side-by-side the prayer made in the suit and submits that the suit under question has been filed by the plaintiff as an Artha Rin Suit in the form of Money Suit for recovery of loan from the Company. He argues that if the Company fails to make the payment against the decree passed in this Money Suit, only then the question of selling the mortgaged property may come up by filing a Mortgage Suit. In the said Mortgage Suit, he submits, the writ petitioner's impleadment might be required if it surfaces that the writ petitioner's deceased-father had mortgaged his personal property and the petitioner inherits the same and, therefore, according to Mr Siddique, the writ petitioner cannot be a necessary party in the present suit and, thus, her name should be struck out from the plaint. 

 29. Let us deal with the questions formulated above. Since there is no scope for the Bank to treat the petitioner and respondent No. 8 as principal-debtor, we are required to see whether the standing of the petitioner and respondent No. 8 fall within the category of indirect mortgagors or guarantors on the basis of their relationship with the deceased-mortgagor. Admittedly, the petitioner and respondent No. 8 are the daughters of the mortgagor who died in the year 2006 and, all of them being Muslim, with the death of their father the provisions of Mahomedan Law comes in operation to regulate all the post-death affairs of the deceased, including preparing an assessment of the wealth left by the deceased, distribution of the deceased's assets and properties among all the heirs of the deceased and making payments of debts. As per the provisions of Mahomedan Law, since this petitioner and respondent No. 8 have inherited the property left by their deceased father-cum-mortgagor, they have, in the eye of law, stepped into the shoes of their deceased father immediately after their father's death for managing and supervising their father's property and, as legal heirs, they are, thus, to shoulder a legal duty to find out as to whether, after paying off the costs and expenses incurred for carrying out the post-death ceremonials as well as the debts payable to any person or institution, there is anything left for them to inherit and enjoy. Unless all the heirs become party to a money-claim from a deceased, the claim cannot be effectively and completely adjudicated upon. In a case like this, if any inheritor is kept outside the suit, two consequences are to inevitably emerge. Firstly, if the Bank is successful in the suit and it reveals that the writ petitioner and respondent No.8 got some Saham in the deceased-mortgagor's property, the decree shall be frustrated because of absence of these two inheritors, namely the writ petitioner and respondent No.8 and, secondly, it will entail multiplicity of suit causing increase in the litigation expenses for the writ petitioner, respondent No.8 and the Bank on top of misusing the invaluable time of the Courts. Thus, the presence of the petitioner and respondent No. 8 in adjudication upon this Artha Rin suit is required for ends of justice and also to prevent the abuse of the process of the Adalat. Accordingly, the submissions of the petitioner's learned Advocate, that the writ petitioner may be added as defendant after becoming a confirmed-inheritor to the deceased's property as the property will devolve upon the petitioner after paying off all the debts and other expenses relating to post-death rituals, appears to us to be devoid of substance. 

 40. Also, the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner that since the suit is for recovery of the loan-money, after the company's failure to comply with the decree passed in this suit when there will be a Mortgage Suit the writ petitioner's liability may come up, appears to us to be misconceived for the' reason that section 5(3) of the Ain, 2003 unambiguously states that all the decree passed in the Artha Rin Suits, other than the Mortgage Suits under the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 or under Order 'XXXIV of the CPC, shall be final decree and, consequently, the writ petitioner and respondent No.8 shall deprive themselves from availing the opportunity to place their case and defend themselves before the Adalat, if they do not appear before the Adalat as defendants. 

 41. Ever since the Artha Rin Ain, 2003 was made operational in the year 2003, the financial institutions introduced institution of Money Suits directly in an expectation of being facilitated towards recovery of their money easily through quick disposal of the suits, as the Artha Rin Suits allow the plaintiffs to straightway sell the mortgaged property without obtaining any preliminary decree, whereas in a Mortgage Suit the plaintiff is required to obtain, at first, a preliminary decree and then by taking some further steps upon obtaining a final decree; the plaintiff becomes able to sell the mortgaged property. Thus, by obtaining a decree in an Artha Rin Suit in the form of a Money Suit, the financial institutions directly obtains an inclusive decree; meaning that they become in a position to-recover their money by adopting a number of means, including selling the mortgaged property directly and, thereafter, selling the other personal property if the sale price of the mortgaged property does not cover the amount of the decree and, if needed; putting the defendants in prison. 

 42. Let us now deal with the submissions' of the learned Advocate for the petitioner that because of impleadment of. the petitioner's name in the category of defendant, she would be subjected to various types of sufferings, in view of section 6(5) which prescribes that all the defendants will be 'jointly' and 'severally' liable. While it is true that the defendants of the Artha Rin suits are jointly and severally liable in the process of implementation of the decree, it does not necessarily mean that the liability of all the defendants are same, for, the liability of the principal-debtor comes first and then comes the liability of the third party mortgagor and lastly the third' party guarantor's liability is to be dealt with towards offsetting the debtor's loan. Similarly, their extent of liability may not be also the same. For example, when some respondents' liability may be 99% of the decretal amount, some of them may incur the liability of only 1 % of the decretal amount. 'Moreover, as per the provision of section 34(2) & 34(4) of the Ain, 2003, there is no scope for the Bank to put the petitioner and respondent No. 8 in civil imprisonment and: thus, the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner about the likelihood of sufferings in civil imprisonment after passing the decree is an apprehension without any legal basis.
